name: Deep Plumbago Blue
lede: Deep Plumbago Blue is a pale, grayed violet-blue named for the plumbago flower, recorded in Ridgway's 1912 atlas and carried into the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 as a pale purple.

sections.title: Named for a garden flower
sections.body:
Our data traces the name to plumbago, a garden flowering shrub whose blooms run from pale to deep blue-violet, a plant-and-landscape word rather than a pigment [1]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas plots it on plate XLIII at hue 53′′′, tone d, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same area as block 227, "pale purple," despite the name's claim to blue [1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 69, chroma 11, hue 291 degrees: light, lightly saturated, and leaning violet more than true blue [1].

Its nearest distinct neighbor by computed color distance is [[deep-greyish-lavender|Deep Greyish Lavender]], 3.7 units away and read in our data as "purpler" [2]. [[manatee|Manatee]] sits a little further, 4.8 units off, called "darker" [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 105, as photographed, more common than 59 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 1.5 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Claude Monet is its most devoted painter here, with the color present in 6 of 50 of his works, more than nine times the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 42 percent of its matches, by lightness rank within the canvas [3].
